traveler: Roger II de Hauteville, King of Sicily
title: The Silver Planisphere and the Porphyry Tomb: from Mileto to Palermo Cathedral
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Boy Count of Mileto and Palermo

stops.name: Mileto, the birth of the great count's last son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the day is standard in modern scholarship. The coordinates are those of the comune of Mileto; the Norman town and its castle were destroyed by the earthquake of 1783 and the modern town rebuilt nearby, so the pin is approximate to the castle site.
stops.campa: In the Norman town of Mileto in Calabria, the seat from which his father took Sicily out of the hands of its emirs island by island, a son is born to Count Roger of Hauteville and Adelaide del Vasto four days before Christmas. The father is near seventy and has spent thirty years at the conquest; the mother is a Piedmontese girl of the Aleramici, his third wife. They give the boy his father's name. Of his infancy the record keeps nothing at all beyond the date. Two elder brothers stand between him and the county.
suggested_refs: The Norman comital seat and abbey of Mileto, destroyed by the earthquake of 1783

stops.name: Mileto, the great count buried
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death and the place; whether the five-year-old was present at the funeral is nowhere recorded and is not claimed here.
stops.campa: Count Roger I dies at Mileto in the summer of the boy's sixth year. He leaves an island held by a few thousand Normans over a population of Greeks, Arabs, Jews and Lombards, and a treasury built on tribute rather than plunder. His elder surviving son Simon takes the county as a child, and Adelaide governs in his name. Nothing records where the younger Roger stands during the burial, or whether he is brought to it at all. He is five years old, and he is third in a line of three.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Count Roger I at the Benedictine abbey of the Santissima Trinita, Mileto

stops.name: Palermo, the mother's regency
stops.date_confidence: attested for Simon's death and Roger's succession in 1105; the month is not recorded and is set to January to order the segment. The court's move from Calabria to Messina and then Palermo is attested as a process, not as a dated event.
stops.campa: Simon dies four years after the father, and the county passes to a nine-year-old. Adelaide del Vasto governs Sicily in his name for seven years, moving the weight of the court off Calabria to Messina and then to Palermo. She keeps on the Greek and Arabic secretaries her husband employed, because the island cannot be taxed or judged in Latin alone. The boy grows up hearing three languages transacted as ordinary business across a chancery floor, and learning that a Norman count in Sicily governs through other men's alphabets.
suggested_refs: The trilingual comital chancery of Sicily under the regency of Adelaide del Vasto

stops.name: Palermo, the dignity out of Constantinople
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month given in the sources consulted, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Alexios I Komnenos, reigning in Constantinople, sends the young count of Sicily the court dignity of protonobilissimos. It is a rank of the Byzantine hierarchy, granted to the son of a Norman adventurer whose family took the island out of Greek and Arab hands within living memory. The empire that once held Sicily now addresses its Latin master in the vocabulary of its own honours. Roger is fourteen, and the rank goes into his style beside the Latin title.
suggested_refs: Byzantine court titles conferred on Norman rulers of the south, eleventh and twelfth centuries

stops.name: Palermo, the Norwegian king in the harbour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The visit of Sigurd Jorsalfare to Sicily is transmitted by Norse saga tradition; the claim that he conferred a royal title is treated by historians as saga material and not as a valid creation of the Sicilian kingship. Roger was a count in 1110 and remained one until 1130. Month unrecorded, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Sigurd Jorsalfare, king of Norway, puts in at Sicily on the way home from Jerusalem with sixty ships and a crusader's reputation. The Norse sagas, written down long afterwards, say that he found a boy ruling the island and made him a king with his own hands, granting the royal title out of the north. Historians treat that coronation as saga material and not as an act with any force in Sicily. Roger is fourteen or fifteen. He is a count, and he will be a count for twenty years yet.
suggested_refs: The saga tradition of Sigurd Jorsalfare's Sicilian landfall, as preserved in the Norse kings' sagas
sources: Wikipedia, 'Roger II of Sicily' (citing saga tradition)

stops.name: Palermo, the charter of the newly knighted count
stops.date_confidence: attested by the date of the charter itself; the charter's text was not independently retrieved in this pass and is known here through the secondary summary.
stops.campa: A charter of the twelfth of June describes him as newly girded with the belt of knighthood and as count of Sicily and Calabria in his own right. The regency is over, and from this document forward every act issued on Sicily carries his name and no one else's. He is sixteen. What comes to him is an island his father conquered and his mother administered, a fleet, a mixed chancery, and the revenues of a customs system the emirs left standing and the Normans never dismantled.
suggested_refs: The comital charter of 12 June 1112, first act of Roger II's personal rule

stops.name: Palermo, the Castilian marriage
stops.date_confidence: the year is not fixed: the sources give 1117 or 1118, and c. 1117 is the safest form. The place of the wedding is nowhere documented; the Palermo pin is an inference from where Roger's household normally resided, and is a gap, not an attested fact. Elvira's mother Isabella is herself disputed, possibly Zaida of Seville.
stops.campa: Roger marries Elvira, daughter of Alfonso VI of Leon and Castile, the king who took Toledo out of Islam and styled himself emperor of all Spain. The bride comes from the far end of the same frontier Sicily sits on, from a court that likewise governs Arabic-speaking subjects through Arabic-speaking clerks. She will bear him four sons and a daughter and will die in the middle of the worst year of his reign. The chroniclers who record the match record nothing whatever of the ceremony.
suggested_refs: The Leonese-Castilian marriage alliance of the Sicilian county, c. 1117
sources: Wikipedia, 'Elvira of Castile, Queen of Sicily'

stops.name: Palermo, the bargain with the duke of Apulia
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year. Where the agreement was concluded is not stated in the sources consulted, which give only 'Apulia/Sicily'; the Palermo pin is an inference from Roger's usual residence and is flagged as such.
stops.campa: William, duke of Apulia and head of the senior Hauteville line, is out of money and out of soldiers. He sells his cousin the count of Sicily what remains of his own rights in the island and in part of Calabria, taking cash and some six hundred knights in exchange. William has no children, and the man buying his rights is twenty-six. The transaction costs Roger a campaigning season's pay and buys him a legal claim on everything the mainland Hautevilles hold whenever the senior line fails.
suggested_refs: The 1122 cession of ducal rights in Sicily and Calabria by Duke William II of Apulia

stops.name: Salerno, the duchy claimed
stops.date_confidence: attested for July 1127 as the month of Duke William's death and of Roger's claim; the sources consulted give only 'Apulia' for the place. Salerno, the ducal capital, is an inference for where the claim was pressed and is flagged as such. Day defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: Duke William dies childless in July and the mainland duchy falls vacant. Roger crosses the straits at once and puts himself forward as the senior surviving Hauteville, claiming Apulia and Calabria by blood. The barons of the south have never been governed from an island and are in no hurry to start. Pope Honorius II, who holds the duchy's overlordship and wants no single Norman ruling from Palermo up to the papal border, rejects the claim, excommunicates him, and preaches against him among those barons.
suggested_refs: The contested Hauteville succession to the duchy of Apulia, 1127-1128

stops.name: Benevento, the pope invests the duke
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1128; day not recorded, defaulted to the first. The general recognition of Roger's ducal authority by the mainland cities and barons follows in September 1129 and is folded into this stop rather than given a pin, the sources naming only 'southern Italy'.
stops.campa: Two campaigning seasons later the coalition has failed to hold, and Honorius comes to Benevento, a papal city standing inside the Norman south, to grant by ceremony what he could not withhold by war. The banner of the duchy of Apulia changes hands; the excommunication lapses; the pope who preached against him confirms his title. Within a year the great mainland cities and the barons who fought him swear to his ducal authority. He is the largest landholder in Italy and still, in name, somebody's vassal.
suggested_refs: The papal investiture of the duchy of Apulia at Benevento, August 1128

stops.name: Palermo Cathedral, the crown on Christmas Day
stops.date_confidence: attested; the bull of Anacletus II is dated 27 September 1130 and the coronation 25 December 1130. Britannica could not be reached to cross-check the naming of Palermo Cathedral specifically (HTTP 403), so the site rests on Wikipedia and the aligned secondary account.
stops.campa: In September the antipope Anacletus II, holding Rome against Innocent II and needing an army, issues a bull erecting Sicily, Calabria and Apulia into a kingdom and Roger into its king. The crown comes from a pope half of Europe calls a usurper: Bernard of Clairvaux is at this moment carrying Innocent II through the courts of France and Germany, and will spend eight years unmaking the papacy that made this king. On Christmas Day Roger is crowned in the cathedral of Palermo and anointed with oil, in a city where the Friday sermon is preached in Arabic.
suggested_refs: The bull of Anacletus II, 27 September 1130, erecting the kingdom of Sicily
sources: bernard_clairvaux.journey.json (the schism of 1130-1138 from the other side)

stops.name: Amalfi, the sea republic brought in
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month recorded in the sources consulted, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Amalfi, which traded with Egypt and Byzantium out of a cliff face and answered to nobody it could not out-sail, refuses the new king. George of Antioch, a Greek from Syria who served the emir of Mahdia before he served Palermo, closes the harbour with the royal fleet while the land forces come down the mountain road. The city submits. Its merchants keep their trade and lose their independence, and the admiral who took it becomes the instrument through which Roger will later reach Africa and Greece.
suggested_refs: The submission of the maritime republic of Amalfi to the Sicilian crown, 1131

stops.name: Capri, the base inside the bay
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the establishment of a naval base on Capri during the 1131 operations is thinly attested and is carried here as tradition. Month is an ordering choice, not a record.
stops.campa: The island in the bay of Naples is taken and held as a station for the fleet working the Campanian coast. He fights the mainland the way an island fights it, cutting the sea road before the land road, so that the barons discover one harvest at a time that their grain and their allies travel at his discretion. From Capri the royal galleys sit inside the enemy's own water, half a day from Naples, half a day from Amalfi, watching every hull that moves between the ports that have not yet submitted.
suggested_refs: The Sicilian royal fleet's forward stations in the Bay of Naples, 1131-1136

stops.name: Cefalu, the vow on the beach
stops.date_confidence: the foundation in 1131 and the mausoleum intent are attested; the storm-and-vow origin is transmitted by the source itself as tradition, not as documentary fact. The porphyry sarcophagi are placed around 1145, when the apse mosaic programme begins. Month is an ordering choice.
stops.campa: The cathedral is begun this year on the shore under the great rock at Cefalu. The tradition attached to the foundation says that a storm drove the king's ship onto this beach and that the building pays a vow made in the water. He intends it for his own tomb and his dynasty's, and has porphyry sarcophagi cut for it, the imperial stone, the stone of Constantinople and of Rome. Greek mosaicists will lay a Christ Pantokrator across the apse in gold. The sarcophagi stand empty here for eighty years.
suggested_refs: The two porphyry sarcophagi commissioned for Cefalu Cathedral, removed to Palermo in 1215

stops.name: Palermo, the chapel inside the palace
stops.date_confidence: attested for the foundation in 1132 on an older chapel, with work continuing through the 1140s and the mosaics only partly finished by 1143. Month defaulted to January; the stop marks a programme, not a single day.
stops.campa: Inside the royal palace he builds the Cappella Palatina onto an older chapel, and gives it exactly the prominence of the throne room, so that the two rooms answer one another across the same floor. The walls take Greek mosaic. The ceiling takes a muqarnas honeycomb of painted wood by Fatimid craftsmen, with drinkers and dancers and hunting scenes looking down into a Latin church. Nothing in the room is a compromise between traditions; each is worked at full strength by men trained in it. A decade on, the mosaics are still unfinished.
suggested_refs: The painted muqarnas ceiling of the Cappella Palatina, Palermo

stops.name: Nocera, the first defeat
stops.date_confidence: attested; the sources give either 24 or 25 July, with 24 July carried by the battle article and by Ranulf II's article against the Roger II article's 25 July. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: Ranulf of Alife, who is the king's brother-in-law, and Robert of Capua bring their knights against him below Nocera and break his line in open field. Roger loses his baggage and most of his cavalry and gets away with a handful of men. He is thirty-six years old and has never lost a battle before. He will lose the next one too. From this year he fights with Muslim infantry and archers out of the Sicilian interior standing in line alongside the Norman horse.
suggested_refs: The battlefield below Nocera, 24 July 1132

stops.name: Salerno, after the field
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1132; the sources give no month for the retreat to Salerno, and August is an ordering choice placing it after Nocera.
stops.campa: He comes into Salerno with what is left of the army and does not go home. The city is the old ducal capital, loyal for the moment, and from inside it he can be seen standing on the mainland at a time when being seen is the whole of the argument. The rebel barons hold Campania and half of Apulia. Roger has an island, a fleet, a treasury none of them can match, and time, which in a war of sieges and harvests belongs to whoever can go on paying through the winter. He begins paying.
suggested_refs: Salerno, ducal capital and royal refuge, 1132 and 1137

stops.name: Palermo, the mantle out of the royal workshop
stops.date_confidence: the inscription dates the piece to AH 528, that is 1133-34; a single day is not recoverable and January 1133 is the ordering choice. The garment cannot have been the actual 1130 coronation robe despite its later use in imperial coronation tradition.
stops.campa: In the tiraz, the palace silk workshop the emirs left behind and the Normans kept running, the weavers finish a red silk mantle for the king. Two lions on it bring down two camels, mirrored across a palm tree, worked in gold thread and pearls. Round the hem runs a band of Kufic Arabic dating the piece to the year 528 of the Hijra and praising not the king by name but the treasury that made it. The robe is a Christian monarch's, and every word woven into it is Arabic.
stops.quote: Here is what was created in the princely treasury, filled with luck, eminence, majesty, perfection, long-suffering, superiority, welcome, prosperity, liberality, brilliance, pride, beauty, the fulfillment of desires and hopes, the pleasure of days and nights, without cease or change, of glory, devotion, preservation of protection, luck, salvation, victory and capability, in the capital of Sicily, in the year 528 H. [1133-1134]
stops.quote_source: Arabic tiraz inscription woven into the coronation mantle, Palermo royal workshop, 528 AH, translation as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Roger II of Sicily', citing Qantara: Mediterranean Heritage
suggested_refs: The red silk mantle of Roger II, Imperial Treasury (Schatzkammer), Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna

stops.name: Palermo, the queen dies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of Elvira's death during an epidemic at the court, and for Roger's own grave illness and the rumours of his death that followed.
stops.campa: An infectious sickness moves through the court in February and Elvira dies of it. Roger falls ill in the same weeks and shuts himself away so completely that nobody outside the palace sees him for months. The rebels on the mainland conclude that he is dead and publish it, and barons who had submitted go over again on the strength of the report. He is forty, he has buried his wife, and his kingdom is being redistributed on the assumption that he has been buried too. He does not marry again for fourteen years.
suggested_refs: The court epidemic of February 1135 and the false report of the king's death

stops.name: Naples, the city that would not fall
stops.date_confidence: corrected from a single 'July 1135 siege': a Pisan fleet arrived in April 1135 with 8,000 men for Robert of Capua and Ranulf, Naples revolted, and the city endured a naval blockade through the spring of 1136, lifted only as Lothair's relief army approached. There is no evidence Roger conducted the blockade in person.
stops.campa: A Pisan fleet lands eight thousand men for Robert of Capua and Ranulf of Alife, and Naples goes over entire. The royal answer is not an assault but a blockade: the fleet across the bay, the roads held, the harvest taken. It runs through the spring and into the following year, and the Neapolitans inside the walls come to real starvation before an imperial army marching down from the north forces the ships off. Duke Sergius VII holds the city through all of it. Two years later he will die fighting on Roger's side.
suggested_refs: The naval blockade of Naples, 1135-1136, and the Pisan expedition of April 1135

stops.name: Messina, the coalition gathering
stops.date_confidence: attested for a return to Messina in late 1135; no day given, and November is an ordering choice within that season.
stops.campa: He crosses back to Messina at the end of the year with the mainland in revolt, the pope excommunicating him, the German and Byzantine emperors in correspondence about him, and Pisa and Genoa hiring their fleets to his enemies. Messina is the kingdom's second city and its gate: from here the straits can be shut and an army put into Calabria in a morning. He spends the winter there building an army again out of Sicilian and African troops. What he said to anyone about his chances that winter, no chronicler wrote down.
suggested_refs: Messina, second city and military gate of the Norman kingdom

stops.name: Bari, the emperor takes the city
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1137 for the siege and capture of Bari by Lothair III's army; day not recorded, defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: Lothair III comes down the Adriatic coast with the German army, Innocent II riding with him and Robert of Capua and Ranulf of Alife guiding him, and takes Bari after a siege. The whole mainland kingdom is gone in a summer. Lothair invests Ranulf with the duchy of Apulia in the pope's presence, and Roger's continental title is extinguished by two of the three powers entitled to grant it. Then the German army, sick and far from home and unwilling to winter in Apulia, turns round and goes back over the Alps.
suggested_refs: The imperial-papal expedition of Lothair III into Apulia, 1137

stops.name: Mercato San Severino, the investiture in the hills
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: an investiture ceremony at San Severino in August 1137 is recorded, but the source detail is thin and no independent confirmation beyond the summary was obtained. Day defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: An investiture is recorded at San Severino in the Campanian hills as he works his way back into the mainland, handing out fiefs to men whose loyalty is a week old and will be tested by December. The German army is already on its road north. Roger has learned what to do with a country that changes sides in a season: come back before the harvest is in, hold a ceremony, write the charters, and let everybody present see who is now in a position to grant land. What was said at San Severino, beyond the fact of it, is not preserved.
suggested_refs: The San Severino investiture of August 1137

stops.name: Tropea, the landing in Calabria
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the disembarkation at Tropea is attested to the year 1137 only. September is an ordering choice placing it after the imperial withdrawal.
stops.campa: He puts his troops ashore at Tropea, on the Calabrian cliff coast, and starts north. The kingdom he is retaking is the kingdom he took ten years ago, from the same barons, with the same arguments, and this time with an army raised largely on Sicilian and North African pay. The fleet moves along the coast beside the marching column. Calabria was his father's country and the province of his own birth, and it comes over to him with very little fighting. By September the road into Campania is open.
suggested_refs: The Calabrian coast road from Tropea to Salerno, campaign of 1137

stops.name: Rignano, the worst day
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the outcome and the death of Sergius VII of Naples. Coordinates corrected to the Balcone delle Puglie escarpment site given by the battle and comune articles.
stops.campa: On the escarpment above the Apulian plain Ranulf of Alife beats him a second time, and far worse. Roger's line breaks; Sergius of Naples, who came over to him after the blockade and is fighting at his side, is killed on the field. The king gets off the mountain with a remnant. His own brother-in-law has now beaten him twice in five years and holds the mainland duchy from the hands of a German emperor. It is the worst day of his reign in the field, and no account of it survives from his own side.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Rignano on the Balcone delle Puglie, 30 October 1137

stops.name: Salerno, the second flight
stops.date_confidence: attested to October or November 1137; the exact day is not recorded and the first of November is an ordering choice.
stops.campa: He comes into Salerno beaten for the second time, by the same coalition, in the same war. No rebuilding speech survives in any source and no ceremony is recorded. What happens instead is arithmetic: Ranulf has won a battle and cannot pay for a second army, the Germans have gone home, Innocent II has no soldiers of his own, and the king of Sicily holds the revenues of the richest island in the Mediterranean and a fleet nobody in Italy can match. He is in the field again before the winter is out.
suggested_refs: Salerno in the winter of 1137, base of the second reconquest

stops.name: Capua, the punishment
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1137 for the devastation of Capua; no month or day is recorded, and mid-November is an ordering choice placing it after Rignano.
stops.campa: Capua is taken and stripped. Robert of Capua, prince of the city, is out of the kingdom for good, and the principality is entered as a title in the royal style, to be given later to one of the king's sons. The war he fights through the rest of this winter is not a war of battles, and every town in Campania will hear how it was fought here before deciding whom to receive in the spring. The crops are burned, the castles pulled down, the estates of men who went over to the emperor confiscated and handed to men who did not.
suggested_refs: The punitive campaign in Campania, winter 1137-1138

stops.name: Alife, the enemy's own ground
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1137 for the devastation of Alife; month and day are not recorded and December is an ordering choice.
stops.campa: Alife is his brother-in-law's town and it is treated accordingly. Ranulf holds Apulia by an emperor's grant and has beaten the king twice in open field, and there is nothing to be done about him in open field; so the king takes his county apart, house by house and harvest by harvest, until the count of Alife has a title and a battle record and no country underneath them. Ranulf will die of a fever at Troia sixteen months from now, undefeated, still holding the duchy nobody could take off him.
suggested_refs: The county of Alife, stronghold of Ranulf II, devastated 1137

stops.name: Troia, the grave opened
stops.date_confidence: Ranulf's death of fever at Troia in April 1139 is attested; the exhumation and reburial come through narrative chronicle sources hostile to Roger and are flagged by those sources as tradition, with no royal record behind them. Day defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: Ranulf of Alife dies of a fever at Troia in April and is buried in the cathedral with the honours of a duke. The chroniclers hostile to Roger report what comes next: that the king arrived at Troia, had the body taken up out of the church and thrown into a ditch outside the walls, and only afterwards, on being reproached, ordered it put back with a decent burial. No royal document mentions any part of it, and the men who wrote it down wanted the king remembered as one who could not let a dead enemy alone. Whether any of it happened cannot now be established.
suggested_refs: The chronicle tradition of the exhumation of Ranulf II at Troia Cathedral

stops.name: Mignano, the captive pope
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the titles and the tribute of 600 schifati; the treaty was signed in Mignano castle. The Galluccio ambush of 22 July was carried out by Roger's son Duke Roger, not by the king in person, and is therefore reported here rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: Innocent II, who excommunicated him in April and invaded the kingdom in July, is ambushed near Galluccio by the king's eldest son and taken prisoner with his cardinals and his treasury. Three days later, in the castle at Mignano, the captive pope recognizes Roger as king of Sicily, duke of Apulia and prince of Capua, against an annual tribute of six hundred schifati. It is the second time a pope has come down into the Norman south to destroy him and gone home again having confirmed his crown.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Mignano, 25 July 1139, signed in Mignano castle

stops.name: Bari, the city retaken
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1139 for the surrender of Bari and the execution of Jaquintus, reportedly by hanging; the month is not recorded and October is an ordering choice after Mignano.
stops.campa: Bari surrenders in the autumn. It had opened its gates to the German emperor two years before and raised up its own leader, Jaquintus, who is now hanged in front of the city that chose him. The city itself is spared a general sack: it is the greatest port on the Adriatic, and its ruin would cost the treasury more than its punishment is worth. The citadel is taken in hand, the port keeps working, and the harbour dues resume in the king's name before the year is out.
suggested_refs: The surrender of Bari and the execution of Jaquintus, 1139

stops.name: Ariano, the assizes and the coinage
stops.date_confidence: attested for an assembly at Ariano in the summer of 1140 and for the reform of the coinage there. Whether the whole surviving law collection was promulgated at this one assembly or compiled across the 1140s is disputed: Falco's contemporary account of the assembly mentions the coinage rather than a complete code. Day defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: He calls the great men of the kingdom, Latin, Greek, Lombard and Norman, to an assembly at Ariano in the Apulian hills, and there reorganizes the currency of the whole realm, calling in the old coinages and issuing a new silver piece struck in his own name. The body of law that carries the name of this place, forty-four surviving clauses on ecclesiastical jurisdiction, property, fiscal right and military obligation, is dated by tradition to these same days. Its prologue argues that a king set over many peoples must give them one law.
suggested_refs: The forty-four surviving clauses of the Assizes of Ariano; the silver ducat of 1140

stops.name: Palermo, the admiral's church and the crown from Christ
stops.date_confidence: attested: founded 1143 by George of Antioch, completed by 1151. Month defaulted to January; the stop marks the foundation and its mosaic programme rather than a single day.
stops.campa: George of Antioch, admiral of the fleet and the second man in the kingdom, founds a church of Greek rite below the palace and has it decorated by mosaicists out of Constantinople. On one wall he sets a panel of the king: Roger in the stiff Byzantine loros and the imperial crown, standing under Christ, who sets the crown on his head with his own hand. No pope appears anywhere in the picture. The inscription beside the figure spells a Latin name in Greek letters, and the admiral is buried in his own church beneath it.
stops.quote_source: Greek-lettered Latin inscription on the coronation mosaic, Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio (the Martorana), Palermo
suggested_refs: The coronation mosaic of Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio, Palermo

stops.name: Palermo, the geographer at the court
stops.date_confidence: attested that al-Idrisi worked at Roger's court for roughly fifteen to eighteen years, c. 1139-1154; no single arrival date is recorded, and 1144 is an ordering choice inside that span. The account of king and geographer conferring rests on Idrisi's own preface taken at face value.
stops.campa: Al-Idrisi, born in Ceuta, of a family claiming descent from the Idrisid sharifs of Morocco, comes to Palermo and stays fifteen years and more. The king sets him a task nobody has attempted: to gather every itinerary, coastline, distance and traveller's report that can be got, to check them against one another, and to make out of them one description of the whole inhabited world. Informants are questioned, sent out, questioned again on their return, and set aside when two of them disagree. Idrisi's preface describes a king who sits in on the checking.
stops.quote: In mathematics, as in the political sphere, the extent of his learning cannot be described. Nor is there any limit to his knowledge of the sciences, so deeply and wisely has he studied them in every particular. He is responsible for singular innovations and for marvelous inventions, such as no prince has ever before realized.
stops.quote_source: al-Idrisi, preface to the Nuzhat al-mushtaq, as translated in 'Al-Idrisi and Roger's Book', Aramco World 28:4 (July/August 1977)
suggested_refs: The preface of the Nuzhat al-mushtaq fi ikhtiraq al-afaq, on the making of the work at Palermo

stops.name: Palermo, the fleet sent to Greece
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1147 for the campaign; Roger neither commanded nor accompanied it, so the pin is Palermo, from which it was directed, and not the Greek coast. Corfu was taken and garrisoned rather than sacked; Thebes and Corinth are securely attested as sacked, while Athens is disputed, listed by the Roger II article and absent from the George of Antioch article. Month defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The admiral sails against the Byzantine empire on the king's warrant, and the king stays in Palermo. Corfu is taken and garrisoned; the fleet works up into the Saronic Gulf and comes home having sacked Thebes and Corinth, the two cities holding the imperial silk monopoly. The weavers of Thebes are shipped back to Sicily with their looms and set to work in the palace tiraz. Within a generation travellers passing through Palermo will report Greek silk workers in the royal workshops, and Greek silk sold under a Norman king's seal.
suggested_refs: Benjamin of Tudela's Palermo notices, c. 1170, recording the Theban silk workers in the royal workshops
The Sicilian raid on Byzantine Greece, 1147
sources: benjamin_de_tudela.journey.json (Palermo and the Theban silk transfer, from the later traveller's side)

stops.name: Palermo, the kingdom of Africa
stops.date_confidence: attested for the capture of Tripoli in 1146 and of Mahdia, Sousse and Sfax in 1148, and for the minting of Arabic gold dinars in Roger's name. The expeditions were led in person by George of Antioch and later Philip of Mahdia; Roger never crossed to Africa, so the pin is Palermo. Month defaulted to January.
stops.campa: From the palace he directs a conquest he never sees. Tripoli falls in 1146 amid famine and civil disorder, Mahdia and Sousse and Sfax two years later, and the emirs of the Ifriqiyan coast take robes and letters of appointment out of Palermo and govern as his deputies. He mints gold dinars in his own name in Arabic and has the Friday prayer said for him in African mosques. The Arab chroniclers who record all this call him the accursed one and describe a Frankish dominion running from Tripoli to the borders of Tunis.
stops.quote: the dominion of the Franks [Normans] extended from Tripoli to the borders of Tunis, and from the western Maghreb to Qayrawan
stops.quote_source: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi al-ta'rikh, translated in David Abulafia, 'The Norman Kingdom of Africa and the Norman Expeditions to Majorca and the Muslim Mediterranean', Anglo-Norman Studies 7 (1985), p. 35
suggested_refs: The Arabic gold dinars struck in Roger's name at Mahdia after 1148
Ibn Abi Dinar, al-Mu'nis fi akhbar Ifriqiya wa Tunis, on the terms imposed on the emir of Mahdia
sources: Romuald of Salerno, Chronicon, on Philip of Mahdia's return to Palermo 'cum triumpho et gloria'

stops.name: Palermo, the heir dies
stops.date_confidence: the date is disputed, given as 2 or 12 May 1148, and the place of death is unknown: the article on Duke Roger says he died an unknown death in an unknown location. The Palermo pin is the court's, not a claim about where he died. William was about seventeen and was crowned co-king at Easter 1151, so the succession narrowed without producing an open crisis.
stops.campa: Duke Roger, the eldest surviving son, the man who took a pope prisoner near Galluccio nine years ago, dies in May. Where he died and of what, nobody wrote down, and even the day is handed down as either the second or the twelfth. Of the four sons Elvira bore, one is now living. What is left of the succession is William, about seventeen, raised to no throne and prepared for nothing, whom the king will crown as co-king within three years. The king is fifty-two.
suggested_refs: Roger III, duke of Apulia, died 2 or 12 May 1148, place unrecorded

stops.name: Palermo, the Burgundian marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1149; the place of the wedding is not documented in the sources consulted and the Palermo pin is an inference from the court's residence, stated here as a gap. Month defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Fourteen years a widower, he marries Sibylla, daughter of the duke of Burgundy, for the plainest of reasons: his sons are dying faster than the kingdom can replace them. He is fifty-four. The bride is brought across Italy to a court whose working languages of administration are Greek and Arabic and whose king has been excommunicated twice by two different popes. Where the wedding was held, who attended it, and what was settled in the contract are not among the things the record troubled to keep. No heir survives it.
suggested_refs: The Burgundian marriage of 1149 and the narrowing of the Hauteville succession

stops.name: Palermo, the third wife
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1151; the place of the wedding is again undocumented and the Palermo pin is inferred. Constance's posthumous birth in November 1154 and her later transmission of the crown to the Hohenstaufen are attested. Month defaulted to January.
stops.campa: Two years on he marries Beatrice of Rethel, out of a family planted in the crusader east. He is fifty-five and she is very young. She will bear him one child, a daughter, born in the November after his death, and that daughter, Constance, will marry a Hohenstaufen and carry Sicily into the German empire, so that the kingdom Roger assembled out of nothing passes in three generations to the house his enemies came from. None of this is known at the wedding.
suggested_refs: Constance de Hauteville, born November 1154, heiress of the Norman kingdom

stops.name: Palermo, the Book of Roger finished
stops.date_confidence: attested: completed AH 548, that is 1153-54, shortly before Roger's death. Seventy regional maps across seven climates are confirmed. The silver planisphere's diameter of about two metres is attested; its weight is contradictory, 300 lb (140 kg) in one article and 450 lb in another citing S. P. Scott, and the contradiction is left standing. Month is an ordering choice.
stops.campa: After some eighteen years the geographer finishes. The Nuzhat al-mushtaq fi ikhtiraq al-afaq, which everybody calls the Book of Roger, cuts the inhabited world into seven climates and each climate into ten sections, and gives seventy regional maps with a description of every one. Beside the book stands the object: a planisphere of solid silver, two metres across, the world engraved on it to Idrisi's design. Nobody who saw the silver disc ever describes it again. The king is fifty-eight and has three weeks to live.
suggested_refs: The Nuzhat al-mushtaq fi ikhtiraq al-afaq, Kitab Rujar, completed at Palermo AH 548
BnF MS Arabe 2221 and Bodleian Pococke 375, the surviving manuscript witnesses

stops.name: Palermo, the death of the king
stops.date_confidence: attested; a few medieval chronological traditions give 27 February, but 26 February is the accepted date. The attribution of the death to exhaustion comes from the chronicler writing under the name Falcandus and no modern medical cause can be recovered.
stops.campa: He dies in the palace on the twenty-sixth of February, fifty-eight years old, twenty-three years a king. The chronicler who writes under the name Falcandus says he was worn out by the immensity of his labours, and no better cause than that can be recovered. He leaves a kingdom that did not exist when he was born, a fleet that has taken cities in Greece and in Africa, a chancery working in three languages, a body of law, and a queen four months pregnant. William is crowned without a war and without a rival.
suggested_refs: The Historia of Hugo Falcandus, on the death of King Roger

stops.name: Palermo Cathedral, the porphyry tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial in Palermo Cathedral in a porphyry sarcophagus and for Frederick II's transfer of the Cefalu sarcophagi to Palermo in 1215; the tomb now stands in the first and second chapels of the right aisle. The exact day of burial is not recorded and is set to the first of March.
stops.campa: They bury him not at Cefalu, where he built for it, but in the cathedral of Palermo, in a sarcophagus of porphyry, the purple stone the Roman and Byzantine emperors kept for themselves. It stands free on the floor under its own canopy, one of the earliest tombs in the Latin west built for a man rather than sunk into a church wall. Sixty years on, his grandson Frederick will have the Cefalu sarcophagi carried to Palermo as well, and will take one of them for himself.
suggested_refs: The porphyry sarcophagi of Palermo Cathedral, right aisle: Roger II, Constance, Henry VI, Frederick II
